analysis.one_liner: Extends Medicaid postpartum coverage to a full year, adds dental care, and pays for it with higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate's final two weeks and referred to the Finance Committee, the bill died without a hearing, a markup, or any vote when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill attacked maternal mortality, which the bill's findings put at about 700 deaths a year, with over 60 percent judged preventable. It extended Medicaid and CHIP coverage for pregnant and postpartum women from 60 days after birth to a full year, required those programs to cover dental care during and after pregnancy, funded state review of every maternal death, funded hospital safety protocols, created training centers on racial bias in maternity care, and let WIC food benefits run two years after birth. To pay for part of it, the bill roughly doubled the federal cigarette tax and raised taxes on other tobacco products so all are taxed at similar rates.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income women on Medicaid and CHIP, who cover a large share of US births and currently lose coverage 60 days after giving birth even though nearly half of maternal deaths happen after that window. Also women of color, who die of pregnancy-related causes at 3 to 4 times the rate of white women, and the families who depend on them. State health departments get funding and data tools to review maternal deaths.

how_it_helps.text: Medicaid and CHIP coverage for pregnant and postpartum women would run a full year instead of ending 60 days after birth, closing a gap that falls in the period when nearly half of maternal deaths occur.

States would be required to cover preventive, diagnostic, periodontal, and restorative dental care for women during pregnancy and the year after, with the federal government picking up 100 percent of the cost of the extended coverage for the first five years and 90 percent after.

The CDC would help states report maternal death data uniformly and issue best practices to state maternal mortality review committees and hospitals, and a new grant program would spread 'maternal safety bundles'—standardized protocols for hemorrhage, hypertension, and other leading causes of death.
New regional centers would train health professionals on implicit bias and cultural competency, aimed at the racial gap in which African-American women die at 3 to 4 times the rate of white women.
The bill raises tobacco taxes, a measure the public-health literature treats as one of the most effective ways to reduce smoking, including smoking during pregnancy.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers, through a doubled federal cigarette tax (from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand) and higher taxes on cigars, pipe tobacco, smokeless tobacco, and other nicotine products—tobacco taxes fall hardest on lower-income people who smoke. Tobacco companies lose sales as prices rise, and retailers face a one-time tax on inventory they hold when the new rates take effect. Federal taxpayers also absorb the cost of the expanded coverage, though the higher tobacco taxes and the 90-percent federal share after year five offset part of it.

drawbacks.text: Tobacco taxes are regressive: they fall hardest on lower-income smokers, the same income group the bill's health coverage provisions help, and the bill roughly doubles the cigarette tax.

The extended coverage and grant programs add new federal spending, authorized at roughly $20 million a year for the grant and training programs plus the cost of a year of postpartum coverage, with the federal share stepping down from 100 percent to 90 percent after five years and leaving states to cover the difference.
States would be barred from tightening Medicaid or CHIP eligibility for pregnant women for five years, a constraint on state budget flexibility that governors of both parties often resist.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but favorable: extending coverage through the postpartum year targets the exact window when nearly half of maternal deaths occur, and the tobacco taxes offset part of the cost while discouraging smoking. The honest objection is that the cigarette tax doubles the burden on low-income smokers on day one; a slower phase-in would have softened that. The bill was also introduced without any estimate of the full federal cost of the coverage extension.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last two weeks of the session, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the MOMMA's Act on December 18, 2018, with eight cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.

The bill would have extended Medicaid and CHIP postpartum coverage from 60 days to one year, required oral health coverage for pregnant and postpartum women, funded state maternal death reviews and hospital safety protocols, and created implicit-bias training centers.

To help pay for it, the bill roughly doubled the federal cigarette excise tax to $100.66 per thousand, raised taxes on cigars, pipe tobacco, smokeless tobacco, and dissolvable tobacco products to similar rates, and indexed all tobacco taxes to inflation.
The Finance Committee took no action on the bill, and there was no vote in either chamber before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies are better off because the bill died: the doubled cigarette tax and tax parity across their products never took effect. Low-income mothers, meanwhile, did not get the extended coverage, and the states did not get the data and funding tools the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies; no extended coverage for mothers

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the MOMMA's Act on December 18, 2018 and managed its referral to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Medicaid and tobacco taxes
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 18, 2018 and never held a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the session twelve days later.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate floor calendar in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor during the lame-duck session in which it was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats—no Republican signed on, and the bill died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill roughly doubles the federal cigarette tax and raises taxes on cigars, pipe tobacco, smokeless tobacco, and dissolvable products to cigarette-equivalent rates, plus a one-time tax on existing inventory. Higher prices would cut sales, and the industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against the public-health purpose of the tax.

Extending postpartum Medicaid coverage to a full year and mandating dental coverage routes more federal dollars through Medicaid plans, with the federal government paying 100 percent of the new extended-coverage cost at first. Their gain runs alongside the enrolled women's gain.

Medicaid and CHIP would be required to cover preventive, diagnostic, periodontal, and restorative dental care for pregnant and postpartum women, turning currently uninsured dental patients into paying ones.

Providers receive grant-funded safety protocols and best-practice guidance and more insured postpartum patients, but also face new standardized protocols and data-reporting expectations aimed at reducing preventable deaths and complications in their delivery rooms.
